A 46-year-old chronic smoker presents with persistent cough,
intermittent fever, hoarseness of voice, and a 6-kg weight loss.
Chest imaging shows a calcified pulmonary lesion with hilar
lymphadenopathy, and serum calcium is elevated. Because
of his smoking history and hoarseness, a bronchogenic
malignancy is initially suspected. However, biopsy of the lymph
nodes reveals the following image. Which of the following is
the most likely underlying diagnosis?
o: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
e:
The smoking history, hoarseness, weight loss, and hypercalcemia may strongly suggest squamous cell carcinoma, making it the tempting choice. However, the biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas, and the combination with hilar lymphadenopathy and hypercalcemia favors sarcoidosis. Key mechanism: Activated macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase, increasing production of active vitamin D and causing hypercalcemia.
• | 「 | Tuberculosis: Classically associated with caseating granulomas.
• | Squamous cell carcinoma: May cause hypercalcemia through parathyroid hormone-related
peptide, but would show keratin pearls.
• | Histoplasmosis: May cause caseating granulomatous inflammation.

Liver biopsy shows bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules.
Which cytokine plays the central role in this process?
e:
Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) is the major cytokine responsible for activating hepatic stellate cells and promoting collagen deposition in chronic liver disease.
• | IL-1: Promotes acute inflammation and fever.
• | TNF-α: Promotes inflammation, hepatocyte injury, and systemic effects.
• | TGF-β: Stimulates stellate-cell activation, collagen synthesis, and fibrosis.
• | IFN-γ: Activates macrophages and promotes Th1-mediated responses; it can inhibit certain
fibrotic pathways.

q:
A 62-year-old man with a long history of smoking presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. He reports dry mouth, constipation, and reduced sweating. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are diminished but become
temporarily stronger after repeated muscle contraction. Muscle strength improves briefly following exercise.Chest imaging reveals a central hilar mass.
Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains his neuromuscular symptoms?
o: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Antibodies against muscle- specific tyrosine kinase receptors
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
e:
The patient has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, commonly associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung. Autoantibodies target presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, causing:
• | ↓ Calcium influx into the presynaptic nerve terminal
• | ↓ Acetylcholine release
• | Proximal muscle weakness
• | Autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth and constipation
• | Reduced reflexes that improve after exercise
Key distinction:
• | Lambert–Eaton: Presynaptic calcium channels; strength improves with repeated use.
• | Myasthenia gravis: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; weakness worsens with repeated use.

immunoglobulin levels are very low. Despite repeated antibiotic and antifungal
treatment, he continues to develop severe infections.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is characterized by severe dysfunction of both:
• | Cell-mediated immunity: T-cell deficiency or dysfunction
• | Humoral immunity: impaired B-cell function and low or ineffective antibody production
Typical findings include:
• | Recurrent severe bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections
• | Persistent oral thrush
• | Chronic diarrhea
• | Failure to thrive
• | Profound lymphopenia
• | Absent or severely reduced thymic shadow
SCID is a medical emergency. Definitive treatment is usually hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.

e: Thromboplastin-rich tissue (from the abrupted placenta) triggers widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, generating innumerable microthrombi throughout the circulation. This process consumes platelets, fibrinogen, and clotting factors faster than they can be replenished — the "consumption coagulopathy" that produces simultaneous thrombosis (microvascular) and hemorrhage (systemic).

mature 8-week scar?
o: Type III collagen has increased further, providing additional tensile strength
Type III collagen has been progressively replaced by type I collagen, which is more cross-linked and tensile
Type IV collagen now predominates, reconstituting the basement membrane
Collagen content decreases overall as the wound matures, reducing tensile strength
e:
types
orlagen (max
Early granulation tissue is rich in type III collagen, laid down by fibroblasts to quickly bridge the wound. Over the following weeks, collagenases remodel this into type I collagen thicker, more heavily cross-linked, and far stronger — which is why tensile strength continues to rise for months even as the wound looks fully healed on the surface (though it never regains more than ~80% of original skin strength).

A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department
with severe retrosternal chest pain for 8 hours. ECG shows
ST-segment elevation. Despite restoration of coronary blood
flow, the affected myocardial cells shows the following
changes as shown in the image.
Which type of necrosis is most likely present?
e: The patient has an acute myocardial infarction due to ischemic injury. In most solid organs, ischemia causes coagulative necrosis, where the basic tissue architecture is temporarily preserved despite cell death. The microscopic clues are increased eosinophilia and loss of nuclei. These are features of irreversible cell injury and necrosis.
